cards.front: An {{c1::epithelium}} is a sheet of cells that covers a surface or lines a tube.
cards.quote: The lining is an epithelium, a sheet of cells that covers a surface or lines a tube.

cards.front: The different proteins and lipids on an epithelial cell's apical and basolateral faces constitute its {{c1::apicobasal polarity}}.
cards.quote: The faces' different proteins and lipids are its apicobasal polarity.

cards.front: Under the usual gut gradients, what orients glucose transport toward the blood, and what does the epithelial seal control?
cards.back: Apical SGLT1 and basolateral GLUT2 orient transport. The seal controls what passes between cells and can leak back.
cards.quote: The seal does not orient that pathway; it decides what can slip between the cells, and so what can leak back.

cards.front: Human SGLT1 expressed in frog oocytes couples each sugar to {{c1::two sodium ions}}.
cards.quote: for human SGLT1 expressed in frog oocytes, coupled transport moves two sodium ions per sugar.
cards.section: How far uphill, and at what cost

cards.front: How do SGLT1, GLUT2 and the sodium-potassium pump differ in their direct roles in intestinal glucose absorption?
cards.back: SGLT1 cotransports sodium and glucose; GLUT2 passively carries glucose down its gradient; the pump maintains the sodium gradient but never transports glucose.
cards.quote: The sodium-potassium pump never touches glucose. Glucose takes the transcellular route, through the cells
cards.section: How far uphill, and at what cost

cards.front: With a sodium concentration factor of 9.3 and a voltage factor of 6.5, about how far uphill can an ideally coupled 1:1 sodium-glucose carrier push glucose?
cards.why: One sodium ion contributes both its concentration and voltage factors.
cards.quote: One sodium per glucose: 9.3 × 6.5 ≈ 61, about 60-fold.
cards.section: How far uphill?

cards.front: If one sodium supplies an approximately 61-fold driving factor, about how far uphill can an ideally coupled 2:1 sodium-glucose carrier push glucose?
cards.why: Each of the two coupled sodium ions contributes the same driving factor.
cards.quote: Two sodium per glucose: the same factor squared, 61 × 61 ≈ 3,700-fold.
cards.section: How far uphill?

cards.front: Why does changing an ideally coupled sodium-glucose carrier from a 1:1 to a 2:1 ratio square its uphill ceiling?
cards.back: Each sodium supplies the same concentration and voltage energy; coupling a second sodium multiplies the first sodium's factor by itself.
cards.quote: A second sodium ion squares the ceiling.
cards.section: How far uphill?

cards.front: In simple accounting, SGLT1 imports two sodium ions per glucose and the pump exports three sodium ions per ATP. What is the ATP cost per glucose?
cards.back: 2 Na⁺ ÷ 3 Na⁺ per ATP = 2/3 ATP per glucose.
cards.quote: In this simple accounting, absorbing one glucose costs about two-thirds of an ATP
cards.section: What does it cost?

cards.front: An intestinal sheet absorbs 1.0 micromole of glucose entirely through 2:1 SGLT1 with no sodium leak. How much sodium enters?
cards.back: 1.0 μmol glucose × 2 μmol Na⁺/μmol glucose = 2.0 μmol Na⁺.
cards.quote: Each glucose brings two sodium ions in, and the pump throws out three sodium ions for each ATP it spends.
cards.section: What does it cost?

cards.front: What distinguishes the transcellular and paracellular routes across an epithelium?
cards.back: The transcellular route passes through cells; the paracellular route passes between them.
cards.quote: Glucose takes the transcellular route, through the cells; the paracellular route runs between them
cards.section: How far uphill, and at what cost

cards.front: SGLT1 is moved from the apical to the basolateral membrane, GLUT2 from the basolateral to the apical membrane, and the sodium pump remains basolateral. Under the usual gradients, how does net glucose movement change and why?
cards.back: It reverses toward the gut. Basolateral SGLT1 uses the sodium gradient to import glucose from blood, while apical GLUT2 permits passive exit into the gut.
cards.quote: A passive carrier moves glucose down whatever gradient it meets; on the basolateral face GLUT2 is an exit under the usual gradient
cards.section: Which face, and why it matters

cards.front: A gut cell adds passive GLUT2 to its apical face while retaining apical SGLT1. What happens early versus late in a meal, and why?
cards.back: Early, apical GLUT2 can increase entry when gut glucose is higher. Later, it can leak glucose back when cellular glucose is higher because it follows either gradient.
cards.quote: A passive carrier moves glucose down whatever gradient it meets
cards.section: Which face, and why it matters

cards.front: A basolateral sodium-potassium pump inhibitor is added to an absorbing intestinal sheet. What happens to lumen-to-blood glucose movement over several minutes, and why?
cards.back: It falls. Intracellular sodium rises, weakening the sodium gradient that supplies energy to apical SGLT1.
cards.quote: the sodium gradient, kept by the pump, supplies the energy
cards.section: Which face, and why it matters

cards.front: Why can adding glucose to oral rehydration solution promote salt and water absorption even while cholera toxin drives secretion?
cards.back: SGLT1 still works: glucose uptake cotransports sodium, and chloride and water follow the absorbed salt.
cards.quote: So the glucose lets the gut absorb salt and water even while the toxin drives secretion.
cards.section: Which face, and why it matters

cards.front: The epithelial seal is the {{c1::tight junction}}, the most apical junction between neighbouring cells.
cards.quote: The seal is the tight junction, the most apical junction between neighbours.
cards.section: The seal: what passes between the cells

cards.front: A protein-sized tracer stops at a tight junction. What does this establish, and what does it not establish?
cards.back: It locates a barrier to that large tracer. It does not establish that ions cannot pass.
cards.quote: That placed a barrier there for a protein-sized tracer. It did not show that the junction is closed to ions.
cards.section: The seal: what passes between the cells

cards.front: Introducing either claudin-1 or claudin-2 into fibroblasts that normally lack tight-junction strands produces branching strands. What conclusion does this support?
cards.back: Either claudin can build tight-junction-like strands in this cell system.
cards.quote: claudin-1 or claudin-2 alone built such strands in mouse L fibroblasts, cells that normally have none.
cards.section: The seal: what passes between the cells

cards.front: Claudin-2 expression lowers MDCK I resistance more than twentyfold without significantly changing strand number. What does the paired result show?
cards.back: Ion permeability depends on which claudins compose the strands, not simply on how many strands are present.
cards.quote: resistance fell more than twentyfold, and strand number did not change significantly.
cards.section: The seal: what passes between the cells

cards.front: Claudin-2 is thought to form a paracellular pore that favours {{c1::cations}}.
cards.quote: Claudin-2 is thought to form a paracellular pore, a channel through the strands that favours cations
cards.section: The seal: what passes between the cells

cards.front: How can a leaky epithelium still block bacteria and large molecules?
cards.back: Its tight junction can contain narrow claudin pores that pass selected small ions and water while strongly restricting large material.
cards.quote: its seal strongly restricts bacteria and large molecules but lets sodium and water through claudin pores.
cards.section: The seal: what passes between the cells

cards.front: Why do ordinary claudin-2 pores mainly affect ions and water accompanying intestinal glucose rather than glucose's net direction?
cards.back: The pores are too narrow even for mannitol, an uncharged molecule about glucose's size; carrier placement and gradients orient glucose transport.
cards.quote: claudin-2 pores do not pass even mannitol, an uncharged molecule about glucose's size.
cards.section: The seal: what passes between the cells

cards.front: TEER (ohm·cm²) = {{c1::(R monolayer − R blank) × area of insert}}.
cards.back: Subtract the filter and fluid resistance before normalizing for area.
cards.quote: TEER (ohm·cm²) = (R monolayer − R blank) × area of insert
cards.section: Measuring the seal: TEER

cards.front: A 1.12 cm² insert reads 3,000 ohm with a control monolayer and 120 ohm blank. Calculate TEER.
cards.section: Measuring the seal: TEER

cards.front: A 1.12 cm² insert reads 250 ohm with a claudin-2 monolayer and 120 ohm blank. Calculate TEER and its fold decrease from 3,225.6 ohm·cm².
cards.quote: Claudin-2: 130 × 1.12 = 145.6 ohm·cm².
cards.section: Measuring the seal: TEER

cards.front: A 0.33 cm² insert reads 400 ohm with a confluent epithelial monolayer and 100 ohm without cells. What is the area-normalized resistance?
cards.quote: Subtract the blank, because the filter and fluid add resistance of their own.
cards.section: Measuring the seal: TEER

cards.front: What does a TEER measurement report, and what important features can it not identify?
cards.back: It reports how easily ions carry current across a sheet. It cannot identify the route or ion, or whether sugars or proteins leak.
cards.quote: It does not say which route or ion, or whether sugars or proteins leak.
cards.section: Measuring the seal: TEER

cards.front: How would dilution-potential measurements distinguish a selective cation pore from a nonselective paracellular leak after claudin-2 expression?
cards.back: Halve salt on one side and calculate sodium-to-chloride permeability. A selective cation pore raises the ratio; a nonselective leak changes it little.
cards.quote: A cation pore predicts a high ratio in claudin-2 cells; a nonselective leak, little change.
cards.section: Design problem: pore or leak?

cards.front: TEER falls after claudin-2 expression. What uncharged-tracer result would support a narrow selective pore rather than a general leak?
cards.back: Mannitol and 4 kDa or larger dextran flux should change little despite increased ion conductance. Increased tracer flux points to a larger leak route.
cards.quote: A narrow pore predicts little change in any of them, since even mannitol is too big for claudin-2 pores.
cards.section: Design problem: pore or leak?

cards.front: How could mutating claudin-2 test whether charged extracellular-loop residues line its cation-selective pore?
cards.back: Neutralize a negative loop charge and measure selectivity. Reduced cation preference would support the claim that the loops line the pore.
cards.quote: if neutralizing a negative charge lowers cation preference, that supports the idea that the loops line the pore.
cards.section: Design problem: pore or leak?

cards.front: Design a controlled cell-culture test of a claudin pore mutation. Which controls are essential, and how far can the conclusion extend?
cards.back: Use parental and empty-vector cells, matched expression, density, culture time and multiple clones. The result establishes behavior in MDCK I, not every intact tissue.
cards.quote: Controls: parental cells and an empty-vector clone, matched expression, cell density and days in culture, and more than one clone.
cards.section: Design problem: pore or leak?

cards.front: Five major claudins are disrupted in MDCK II cells: strands vanish and resistance falls, but polarity remains organized. What does this show, and what alternative remains?
cards.back: Claudin strands were not required for polarity in these cells. Other claudins or remaining JAM-A contacts could still provide a fence.
cards.quote: They did not rule out other claudins, and membrane contacts containing JAM-A remained
cards.section: Is the seal also a fence?

cards.front: In the standard epithelial polarity scheme, the {{c1::Crumbs complex}} sits apically.
cards.quote: The Crumbs complex sits apically.
cards.section: How each cell knows its top from its bottom

cards.front: In the standard epithelial polarity scheme, the {{c1::Par complex}} marks the apical-lateral boundary.
cards.back: It includes the kinase aPKC.
cards.quote: The Par complex, which includes the kinase aPKC, sits at the boundary where apical meets lateral.
cards.section: How each cell knows its top from its bottom

cards.front: In the standard epithelial polarity scheme, the {{c1::Scribble complex}} sits basolaterally.
cards.quote: The Scribble complex sits basolaterally.
cards.section: How each cell knows its top from its bottom

cards.front: How do polarity complexes and polarized membrane traffic keep epithelial faces compositionally distinct?
cards.back: The complexes are thought to restrain one another to maintain territories; polarized traffic then delivers appropriate proteins to each face.
cards.quote: The groups are thought to restrain one another, so each holds its own territory
cards.section: How each cell knows its top from its bottom

cards.front: An adherens junction uses E-cadherin and catenins to mechanically couple neighbouring cells' belts of {{c1::actin}}.
cards.quote: Below the seal, more junctions are stacked down the side of the cell in a characteristic order
cards.section: Holding the sheet together: the rest of the stack

cards.front: The junction that ties keratin intermediate filaments of neighbouring epithelial cells together is the {{c1::desmosome}}.
cards.back: It acts as a spot weld that resists stretching and tearing.
cards.quote: The faces and the seal matter only while the sheet stays in one piece.
cards.section: Holding the sheet together: the rest of the stack

cards.front: Animal {{c1::gap junctions}} pass ions and small molecules directly from cytosol to cytosol.
cards.quote: Gap junctions are not alike. Channels made of different connexins pass the messenger cAMP very differently relative to potassium
cards.section: Junction details

cards.front: How do desmosomes and hemidesmosomes differ in what they anchor?
cards.back: Desmosomes link keratin networks between neighboring cells; hemidesmosomes anchor basal keratin to the basement membrane.
cards.quote: The faces and the seal matter only while the sheet stays in one piece.
cards.section: Holding the sheet together: the rest of the stack

cards.front: How does a plant plasmodesma differ structurally from an animal gap junction?
cards.back: A plasmodesma is a plasma-membrane-lined channel through the wall with an ER desmotubule; cytosol occupies the surrounding sleeve.
cards.quote: Down its middle runs the desmotubule, a narrow strand of endoplasmic reticulum continuous with the ER of both cells.
cards.section: Plants: walls and plasmodesmata

cards.front: At a plant-cell interface, a mutant lacks plasmodesmata with a visible cytoplasmic sleeve, yet GFP crosses faster than in wild type. What conclusion is justified?
cards.back: Visible sleeve morphology does not reliably predict transport: a pore without a visible sleeve passed protein at this interface.
cards.quote: A pore with no visible sleeve still passed protein, at least at this interface.
cards.section: A pore with no visible sleeve
